translations.text: There was a man from Ramathaim-zophim, in the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives. One was named Hannah, and the other was named Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
This man would go up from his town from time to time to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts at Shiloh. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were there as priests of the Lord.
One day, when Elkanah offered a sacrifice, he gave portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But he gave Hannah a double portion, because he loved Hannah, though the Lord had closed her womb.
Her rival would provoke her severely to distress her, because the Lord had closed her womb.
Peninnah did this year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the house of the Lord, Peninnah would provoke her like this, and Hannah would weep and refuse to eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Hannah, why are you crying? Why have you not eaten? Why is your heart sad? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
Hannah got up after she had eaten and drunk at Shiloh, and went up to the house of the Lord. Eli the priest was sitting on a chair at the threshold of the Lord’s temple.
She was deeply distressed and prayed before the Lord, weeping bitterly.

She made a vow and said, “Lord of hosts, if you will indeed look upon your servant’s affliction and remember me, and not forget your servant, but give your servant a son, I will give him to the Lord for all the days of his life, and no razor will touch his head.”
As she continued praying before the Lord, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was speaking only in her heart. Her lips were moving, but her voice could not be heard, so Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, “How long will you remain drunk? Let your wine wear off.”
Hannah answered him, “No, my lord. I am a woman deeply troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the Lord.
Do not regard your servant here before you as a wicked woman. I have been speaking all this time out of my great distress and anguish.”
Eli answered her, “Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant the request you have made of him.”
She said, “May your servant find favor in your eyes.” Then the woman went on her way, and her face was no longer troubled.
They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the Lord. Then they returned to their home at Ramah. Elkanah slept with his wife Hannah, and the Lord remembered her.
In time, Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, because she had asked the Lord for him.
Elkanah and his entire household went up to offer the Lord the annual sacrifices he had vowed.
But Hannah did not go up, because she had said to her husband, “When the boy is weaned, I will bring him, and he will appear before the Lord and remain there forever.”
Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Do what seems good to you. Stay until you have weaned him. Only may the Lord confirm your word.” So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, one seah of flour, and a skin of wine. She brought him to the house of the Lord at Shiloh. The boy was still young.
They slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli.
Hannah said to Eli, “Please, my lord! As surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you, praying before the Lord.
It was for this boy that I prayed, and the Lord granted me the request I made of him.
And I too have lent him to the Lord for all the days he lives, for he was granted to me at my request from the Lord. And they worshiped the Lord there.
Hannah prayed and said, “My heart has grown strong in the LORD, and my horn has been raised. My mouth has opened against my enemies, because you have made me rejoice in your salvation.”
There is no one holy like the Lord, for there is no one besides you, and there is no one mighty like our God.
Do not keep speaking boastfully, and do not let abusive speech come from your mouths, for the Lord has knowledge, and schemes cannot succeed before him.
The bows of mighty warriors will be broken, and the weak have been made strong.

Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have become prosperous. The barren woman has given birth and is satisfied, while the woman with many children has become desolate.
The Lord puts to death and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.
The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and also lifts up.

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dung heap, to seat them with nobles and give them a throne of honor as their inheritance. The Lord [?] the depths of the earth and set the world upon them.
He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked will be silenced in darkness, for a warrior does not prevail by his own strength.

The Lord will shatter those who provoke him, and he will thunder against them in heaven. The Lord will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to his king and raise the horn of his anointed one.
Elkanah went home to Ramah, he and his wife Hannah, while the boy Samuel served before the Lord under Eli the priest.
Eli’s sons were sinful men; they did not know the Lord.

They made themselves a three-pronged fork and took the priests’ portion from the people, from everyone who offered a sacrifice. When the meat was cooking, the priests’ servant would come with a three-pronged fork in his hand.
He would thrust it into the basin, kettle, cauldron, or pot, and whatever the fork brought up, the priest would take for himself. This is what they did to all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh.

Even before they offered the sacrificial offerings, the priests’ servant would come and say to the person offering the sacrifice, “Give meat to roast for the priests. I will not take cooked meat from you, only raw meat.”
The man would say to him, “Let them make the offering today, and then take as much as you desire.” But he would reply, “You must give it now, or else I will take it by force.”
The sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, because they angered people before the Lord.
The boy Samuel served before the Lord, wearing a linen ephod.
His mother made him a little robe and brought it up to him from time to time when she went up with her husband to offer the sacrifices she had vowed.
Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife and said, “May the Lord give you offspring by this woman in place of the one you lent to the Lord.” Then they went home.
The Lord attended to Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew up before the Lord.
Eli was very old, and he heard everything his sons were doing to all Israel, and that they were dishonoring the women who prayed at the tent of meeting.
He said to them, “Why do you do such things? I hear bad reports about you from all these people.
No, my sons! This report I hear is not good: you are leading the Lord’s people astray.

If a person sins against another person, he can appeal to the Lord. But if a person sins against the Lord, to whom can he appeal?” Yet they did not listen to their father, because the Lord wanted to put them to death.
The boy Samuel continued to grow greatly and found favor before the Lord and also before other people.
A man of the Lord came to Eli and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: I certainly revealed myself to your father’s household when they were in Egypt, in Pharaoh’s household.

I chose him for myself from all the tribes of Israel to be a priest, to go up to my altar, to offer incense before me, and to wear the ephod. I gave your father’s household all the offerings of the Israelites.

Why have you acted arrogantly toward my sacrifices and my offerings, which I commanded in the wilderness? You have honored your sons more than me, choosing for yourselves the best of all the offerings of my people Israel.

Therefore this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I certainly said that your household and your father’s household would serve before me forever. But now the Lord says: Far be it from me! I will honor those who honor me, but those who despise me will be disgraced.
Look, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will cut off your arm and your father’s arm, and there will be no old man in your household.
And [?] distress will grip your dwelling amid all the good done in Israel, and there will never be an old man in your household.
Yet I will not remove every man of yours from my altar, so that your eyes may grow dim and your soul waste away. All the offspring of your household will die as grown men.
This will be the sign for you, which will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: both of them will die on the same day.

I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, one after my own heart. He will do what is in my heart and in my soul. I will build him an enduring household, and he will walk before [?] my anointed one all his days.
Everyone left in your household will come and bow down to him for a silver coin and a loaf of bread, and will say, ‘Send me to one of the priests so that I may eat a mouthful of bread.’”
The boy Samuel was serving before the Lord under Eli the priest. The word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no revealed vision.
In those days, Eli was lying down in his place. His eyes had begun to grow dim, and he could not see.
The lamp of the Lord had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the Lord’s temple, where the ark of God was.
The Lord called Samuel, and he said, “Here I am.”
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, because you called me.” But he said, “I did not call. Go and lie down.” So he went and lay down.
The Lord called Samuel again. Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, because you called me.” He said, “I did not call, my son. Go and lie down.”
Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him.
The Lord called Samuel again, for the third time. Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, because you called me.” Then Eli realized that the Lord was calling the boy.
Eli said to Samuel, “Go and lie down. If he calls you, say, ‘Speak, Lord, because your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The Lord came and stood there and called twice, “Samuel, Samuel!” Samuel said, “Speak, Lord, because your servant is listening.”
The Lord said to Samuel, “Look, I am doing something in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears about it ring.
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken concerning his household, from beginning to end.
I will tell him that I am judging his household forever because of the wrongdoing he knew about: his sons were insulting the people, and he did not rebuke them.
Therefore I have sworn concerning Eli’s household that the wrongdoing of Eli’s household will never be atoned for by sacrifices or offerings.”
Samuel lay down until morning, and then opened the door of the Lord’s house. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
Eli called Samuel and said, “Samuel, my son.” He answered, “Here I am.”

He said to him, “What was the message the Lord spoke to you? Do not be afraid to tell me. May God do this to you, and more besides, if you hide from me a single word of everything the Lord said to you.”
Samuel told him everything and concealed nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the LORD. Let him do whatever seems good to him.”
Samuel knew that the Lord was with him and did not let any of his words fall to the ground.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel had been confirmed as a prophet of God.
The Lord continued to reveal himself at Shiloh through his words.
Samuel’s word came to all Israel. Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and camped at the Stone of Help, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines drew up their ranks against Israel, and battle began. Israel was defeated before the Philistines, and about four thousand men were killed in the battle line in the field.

When the people came back to the camp, the elders of Israel said, “Why has the Lord defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the Lord of Hosts here from Shiloh, so that it may go among us and save us from the power of our enemies.”

The people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of Hosts, who is enthroned upon the cherubim. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of the Lord.
When the ark of the covenant of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel gave a great shout, and the earth shook.
The Philistines heard the sound of the shouting and said, “What is this sound of shouting in the Hebrews’ camp?” Then they learned that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp.
The Philistines were afraid, for they said, “God has come into the camp!” They said, “Woe to us! Nothing like this has happened before.
Woe to us! Who will rescue us from the hands of this mighty God? This is the God who struck all Egypt with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Be strong and be men, Philistines, so that you do not become slaves to the Hebrews as they were slaves to you. Be men and fight them!”
The Philistines fought against Israel, and Israel was defeated. Everyone fled to his tent. There was a very great slaughter in Israel, and thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fell that day.
The ark of the Lord was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
A man from the tribe of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh that day with his clothes torn and dirt on his head.
Eli was sitting on a chair beside the road, watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. The man came to report the news in the town, and the whole town wailed.
Eli heard the sound of wailing and said, “What is this sound of commotion?” The man hurried over and told Eli.
Eli was seventy-eight years old. His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see.
The man said to Eli, “I have come from the battle line. I fled from the battle line and came here today.” Eli said to him, “What is the news, my son?”

The messenger answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, have also died, and the ark of God has been captured.”
When Eli remembered the ark of God, he fell backward from his chair beside the gate. His neck broke, and he died, because he was an old and heavy man. He had judged Israel for forty years.

His daughter-in-law, Phinehas’s wife, was pregnant and close to giving birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband had died, she knelt down and gave birth, for her labor pains had come upon her.
As she was dying, the women standing over her said, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son.” But she did not answer or pay attention.
She named the boy Ichabod and said, “Glory has departed from Israel,” because the ark of God had been captured, and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
She said, “Glory has departed from Israel, because the ark of the Lord, the God of Israel, has been captured.”
The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
The Philistines took the ark of God, brought it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon.
The people of Ashdod rose early the next day and found Dagon lying face down on the ground before the ark of God. They took Dagon and put him back in his place.

They rose early the following morning, and there was Dagon lying face down on the ground before the ark of the Lord. Dagon's head and both his hands were cut off on the threshold of the doorway. Only Dagon's body remained.
That is why the priests of Dagon and everyone entering Dagon's temple in Ashdod do not step on the threshold to this day.
The Lord's hand weighed heavily on the people of Ashdod. He devastated them and afflicted them with hemorrhoids, both in Ashdod and its surrounding territory.
When the people of Ashdod saw what had happened to them, they said, "The ark of the Lord, the God of Israel, must not remain with us, because his hand weighs heavily on us and on Dagon our god."

They sent for all the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together. They said, "What shall we do with the ark of the Lord, the God of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the Lord, the God of Israel, be moved to Gath." So they moved the ark of the Lord, the God of Israel.
After they moved it, the Lord's hand struck the city with a very severe plague. He struck the people of the city, from the least to the greatest, and hemorrhoids broke out on them.
They sent the ark of God to Ekron. The people of Ekron cried out, saying, "They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us to kill us and our people!"

They sent for all the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together. They said, "Send the ark of the God of Israel away, and let it return to its own place so that it does not kill us and our people." For deadly panic had spread throughout the city, and God's hand weighed very heavily there.
The people who did not die were afflicted with hemorrhoids, and the city's cry rose to heaven.
The ark of the Lord remained in the land of the Philistines for seven months.
The Philistines summoned the priests and the rulers and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the Lord? Tell us what we should send with it when we return it to its place."

They said, "If you send away the ark of the Lord, the God of Israel, do not send it empty. Be sure to bring offerings for it. Then you will be healed, and you will learn why the Lord's hand has not withdrawn from you."

They asked, "What offerings should we bring for it?" They answered, "Five gold hemorrhoids and five gold mice, corresponding to the number of the Philistine rulers, because the same plague is on you and your rulers.
Make images of your hemorrhoids and images of your mice that are destroying the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand upon you, your god, and your land.
Do not harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs. After they had been made a mockery of, did they not send the people away, so that they left?
Now make a new cart and take two nursing cows that have never been yoked. Harness the cows to the cart, and take their calves away from them and back home.
Take the ark of the Lord and put it on the cart. Put the gold objects that you bring as offerings for it in a chest beside it. Then send it off and let it go.

Watch: if it goes along the road leading up toward its own territory, to Beth-shemesh, then it was the Lord who brought this great disaster upon us. Otherwise, we will know that it was not his hand that struck us, but that this happened to us by chance."
The men did this. They took two nursing cows and harnessed them to the cart, and they shut their calves up at home.
They put the ark of God on the cart, along with the chest, the gold mice, and the images of their hemorrhoids.

The cows set out on the road toward the territory of Beth-shemesh. They followed a single path, lowing as they went, and did not turn aside to the right or the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed them as far as the territory of Beth-shemesh.
The people of the town of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. They looked up and saw the ark, and they rejoiced when they saw it.
The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A large stone was there. They split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.

The Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the chest beside it, which contained the gold objects, and placed them on the large stone. The people of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices to God that day.
The five rulers of the Philistines saw this and returned to Ekron that same day.
These are the gold tumors that the Philistines brought as an offering to God: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.

There was one gold mouse for each of all the towns of the Philistines and their five rulers, from the fortified cities to the unwalled villages, and as far as Abel the Great, on which they placed the ark of the LORD. It remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.

The LORD struck the people of Beth-shemesh because they feared the ark of the LORD. The LORD struck down five thousand and seventy men among the people. The people mourned because the LORD had struck them with a great blow.
The people of Beth-shemesh said, “Who can stand before the LORD, this holy God? Who will take the ark up away from us?”
They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim and said, “The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to your town.”
The men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD. They brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill. He consecrated his son Eleazar, who guarded the ark of the LORD.
From the day the ark settled in Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, about twenty years. The whole house of Israel devoted themselves to following the LORD.

Samuel said to the whole house of Israel, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, remove the foreign gods and the female idols from among you. Set your hearts on the LORD and serve him alone, and he will rescue you from the power of the Philistines.”
The Israelites removed Baal and the sacred groves and served the LORD alone.
Samuel said, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray for you before the LORD.”
They gathered at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the LORD. They fasted that day and said, “We have sinned against the LORD.” Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
The Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, and the rulers of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the Israelites heard about it, they were afraid of the Philistines.
The Israelites said to Samuel, “Do not stop praying for us before the LORD our God, so that he may save us from the power of the Philistines.”
Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. Samuel prayed before the LORD for the Israelites, and the LORD answered him.

While Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines approached to fight against the Israelites. But that day the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel.
The men of Israel went out from Mizpah, pursued the Philistines, and struck them down as far as the area below Beth-jeshan.
Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Beth-jeshan. He named it “Stone of Help,” saying, “The LORD has helped us this far.”
The Philistines were defeated and did not come into Israel’s territory again. The LORD’s hand was against the Philistines throughout Samuel’s lifetime.

The towns that the Philistines had taken from Israel were returned to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, together with their territories. The LORD rescued Israel from the power of the Philistines, and there was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged the Israelites throughout his life.
Year after year he traveled on a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel in all these places.
He would return to Ramah, because his home was there. There he judged Israel, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
His firstborn son was named Joel, and his second was named Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba.
His sons did not follow his ways. They turned aside to deceit, accepted bribes, and perverted justice.
All the elders of the Israelites gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him, “Look, you have grown old, and your sons do not follow your ways. Now give us a king to judge us like all the nations.”
Samuel was displeased when they said to him, “Give us a king to judge us like all the nations.” So Samuel prayed before the Lord.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to the people in everything they say to you, because they have not rejected you; they have rejected me from being king over them.
Just as they have done from the day I brought them up from the land of Egypt until today, abandoning me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you as well.
Now listen to them, but solemnly warn them and explain to them the way the king who reigns over them will rule.”
Samuel told all the Lord’s words to the people who were asking him for a king.
He said, “This will be the way the king who reigns over you will rule: he will take your sons and assign them to his chariots and his cavalry, and they will run before his chariots.

He will appoint for himself commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten. They will plow his fields, reap his harvest, and make his weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters to be weavers, grain grinders, and bakers.
He will take your good fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your crops and vineyards and give it to his trusted officials and his servants.
He will take your male servants, your female servants, your finest troops, and your donkeys and put them to his work.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves.
On that day you will cry out because of the king you have chosen for yourselves, but the Lord will not answer you on that day.”
But the people refused to listen to Samuel. They said to him, “No! We must have a king over us,
so that we too may be like all the nations. Our king will judge us, go out before us, and fight our battles.”
Samuel heard everything the people said and repeated it before the Lord.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to them and appoint a king for them.” Then Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Go, each of you, to your own town.”
There was a man from Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zerod, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite and a mighty warrior.
He had a son named Saul, a handsome man. There was no man among the Israelites more handsome than he was, and he stood head and shoulders above all the people.

The female donkeys belonging to Kish, Saul’s father, went missing. Kish said to his son Saul, “Take one of the young servants with you, get up, and go look for the donkeys.” So Saul got up and went, taking one of the young servants with him, and set out to look for his father’s donkeys.

He passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Gomra, but did not find them. He passed through the land of Taala, but they were not there. He passed through the land of Benjamin, but did not find them.
They came to the land of Zur, and Saul said to the young servant with him, “Come, let us go back, or my father may stop worrying about the donkeys and become anxious about us.”

His young servant said to him, “Look, there is a man of God in this town, a man highly respected by the people. Everything he says certainly comes true. Let us go there now. Perhaps he will show us the way we should take.”
Saul said to his young servant, “If we go, what shall we bring to the man of God? The bread in our bags is gone, and there are no provisions to bring to the man of God, for we have nothing.”
The servant spoke again to his master and said, “Look, I have a quarter of a shekel of silver with me. Let us give it to the man of God, and he will show us our way.”
For in former times in Israel, when someone went to inquire of God, he would say, “Come, let us go to the seer,” because the person now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.
Saul said to his servant, “What you say is good. Come, let us go.” So they went to the town where the man of God was.
As they were going up the slope to the town, they found young women coming out to draw water. Saul said to them, “Is the seer here?”
The women answered, “Yes, he is just ahead of you. Go up quickly now, because he has come to the town today, for the people have a sacrifice today at the high place.”

“When you enter the town, you will find him right away, before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people do not eat until he comes, because he blesses the sacrifices; afterward, those who have been invited eat. Now go up, because you will find him today.”
They went up to the town. As they were entering the town, Samuel came out toward them on his way up to the high place.
A day before Saul came, the LORD had spoken to Samuel, saying:

“About this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. Anoint him as ruler over my people Israel. He will save my people from the power of the Philistines, for I have seen my people, and their cry has reached me.”
Samuel saw Saul, whom the LORD had chosen, and the LORD said to Samuel, “Here is the man I told you about. This man will govern my people.”
Saul approached Samuel inside the gateway and said, “Tell me, where is the seer’s house?”
Samuel answered Saul, “I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place and eat with me today. I will send you on your way in the morning and tell you everything that is in your heart.

As for the donkeys you lost three days ago today, do not worry about them, because they have been found. And to whom does all the desire of the house of Israel belong, if not to you and your father’s household?”
Saul answered Samuel, “Look, I am a Benjaminite, from the smallest of Israel’s tribes, and my clan is the least of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin. Why have you said this to me?”
Samuel took Saul and his servant, brought them into the house, and gave them places at the head of the invited guests, who numbered about thirty men.
Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you, which I told you to set aside.”

The cook lifted up the thigh and the upper portion and placed them before Saul. He said, “Here is what was kept back. Set it before you and eat, because it has been reserved for you for this occasion.” So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
He came down from the high place to the town and spoke with Saul on the roof.
He rose early, as dawn was breaking, and Samuel called to Saul on the roof and said, “Get up, so I can send you on your way.” Saul got up, and the two of them, he and Samuel, went outside.
As they were going down to the edge of the town, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us, but you stand here for now, and I will make God’s word known to you.”
Samuel took a horn of oil, poured it on Saul’s head, kissed him, and said to him, “The LORD has anointed you as ruler over his inheritance.

When you leave me today, you will find two men beside Rachel’s tomb, in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah. They will tell you, ‘The donkeys you went to look for have been found. Your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and is worried about you, saying, “What shall I do about my son?”’

When you go on farther from there and reach the terebinth of Tabor, you will find three men going up to God at Bethel. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a skin of wine.
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, and you are to accept them from their hands.

Afterward you will come to the hill of God, where the Philistine garrison is. When you reach the town there, you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place, with lyres, harps, [?], and [?] ahead of them, while they prophesy.
The Spirit of the LORD will come powerfully upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be changed into a different man.
When these signs come upon you, do whatever you are able to do, because God is with you.
Go down ahead of me to Gilgal. I will come down to you there to offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and tell you what to do.
When he turned to leave Samuel, God gave him a different heart, and all these signs came about that day.
He came to Ramah, and a band of prophets met him. The Spirit of God came powerfully upon him, and he prophesied among them.
All who had known him previously saw him prophesying with the prophets. The people said to one another, “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
A man from there answered, “Who is his father?” Because of this, it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
They finished prophesying, and Saul came from [?].
Saul’s uncle said to him and his servant, “Where did you go?” He answered, “To look for the donkeys. When we saw that they were not there, we went to Samuel.”
Saul’s uncle said to him, “Tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul said to his uncle, “He told me plainly that the donkeys had been found.” But he did not tell him about the matter of the kingship, of which Samuel had spoken to him.
Samuel gathered the people before the Lord at Mizpah.

He said to the Israelites, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought Israel up from the land of Egypt and rescued you from the power of the Philistines and from the power of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and distress, and you have said, ‘No! Set a king over us instead.’ Now let your tribes and your thousands stand before the Lord.”
Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected.
He brought forward the tribe of Benjamin by its clans, and the clan of Matri was chosen. Saul son of Kish was chosen, but when they looked for him, he could not be found.
Samuel again inquired of the LORD and said, “Where is this man?” The LORD said to Samuel, “He is hiding among the baggage.”
They ran and brought him from there. He stood among the people, and he was taller than all the people by a head and shoulders.
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one God has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” Then all the people shouted, “Long live the king!”
Samuel explained to the people the law governing the king, wrote it in a book, and placed it before the Lord. Then Samuel sent all the people away, and everyone went home.
Saul also went home to Ramah, and a band of men whose hearts God had touched went with him.
But some wicked men said, “How can this man save us?” They despised him and brought him no gifts, but he remained silent.
Nahash the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Lachish in Gilead. All the men of Lachish said to Nahash, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”
Nahash the Ammonite said to them, “I will make a treaty with you on this condition: you must put out all your right eyes, and I will make this a disgrace upon all Israel.”
The elders of Lachish said to him, “Give us seven days to send messengers throughout the territory of Israel and see whether anyone will rescue us. If not, we will come out to you.”
The messengers came to Ramah of Saul and reported these words before the people. All the people raised their voices and wept.
Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen. He asked, “What is wrong with the people? Why are they weeping?” They told him what the men of Lachish had said.
The Spirit of God came powerfully upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger burned fiercely.

He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them throughout the territory of Israel by messengers, saying, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not come out to follow Saul and Samuel.” The fear of God fell upon the people, and they all came out as one man.
He counted them at Bezek. There were three hundred thousand Israelites and thirty thousand men of Judah.

They said to the messengers who had come from Lachish, “Tell the men of Lachish and Gilead, ‘Tomorrow, when the sun grows hot, you will be delivered.’” The messengers came and told the people of Lachish, and they rejoiced.
The people of Lachish said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you.”

The next day, Saul divided the people into three companies. He entered the camp during the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the day grew hot. Those who remained were scattered, so that no two of them could be found together.
The people said to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Hand those men over to us, and we will put them to death.”
Saul said, “No one shall be put to death today, because today the Lord has brought deliverance to Israel.”
Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.”

All the people went to Gilgal, and there at Gilgal they made Saul king before the Lord. There they offered sacrifices of peace offerings before the Lord, and Saul and all the people of Israel rejoiced greatly there.
Samuel said to all Israel, “Look, I have listened to you in everything you said to me, and I have appointed a king over you.”
“Now look, the king is before you. I have grown old and advanced in years, and my sons are here with you. I have led you from my youth until today.”

“Here I stand before you. Testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed one. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I wronged? Whom have I oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes because of it? Tell me, and I will repay you.”
They said to him, “You have not wronged us or oppressed us, nor have you taken anything from any of us.”
He said to them, “God is a witness against you, and his anointed one is a witness against you today, that you have found nothing in my hands.” They said, “He is a witness.”
Samuel said to the people, “The Lord alone is God, who raised up Moses and Aaron and brought our ancestors up from the land of Egypt.
“Now stand here, and I will plead my case with you before the Lord concerning all the righteous deeds he has done for you and your ancestors.
“When Jacob entered Egypt, your ancestors prayed before the Lord. The Lord sent Moses and Aaron, brought your ancestors up from the land of Egypt, and settled them in this place.
“But they forgot the Lord their God, and he handed them over to Sisera, the commander of Hazor’s army, to the Philistines, and to the king of Moab, who fought against them.

“They prayed before the Lord and said, ‘We have sinned, because we have abandoned the Lord our God and served Baal and the sacred groves. Now rescue us from the power of our enemies, and we will serve you.’
“The Lord sent Deborah, Barak, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson, and rescued you from the power of your enemies all around you, and you lived in peace.
“You saw Nahash, king of the Ammonites, coming against you, and you said, ‘No, a king must reign over us,’ although the LORD your God was your king.”
“Now here is the king you chose and asked for. Look, the Lord has given you a king.
“If you fear the Lord, serve him, obey his voice, and do not provoke him, then both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the Lord your God.
“But if you do not obey the voice of the Lord your God and provoke him, the Lord’s hand will be against you, as it was against your ancestors.
“Now get ready and see this great thing that the Lord is about to do before you.
“Look, it is wheat harvest today. I will call upon the Lord, and he will send thunder and rain. Know and see how great your wickedness is in asking for a king for yourselves.”
Then Samuel called upon the Lord, and the Lord sent thunder and rain in that place. All the people were greatly afraid of the Lord and of Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray for your servants before the Lord your God, so that we do not die, because we have added to all our sins the great evil of asking for a king for ourselves.”
Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil, but do not turn away from following the Lord. Instead, serve the Lord with all your heart.
“Do not turn aside to follow worthless things, so that you do not die. They cannot rescue you, because they are worthless.”
For the LORD will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name, because he was pleased to make you his people.
As for me, far be it from me to sin against the Lord by failing to pray for you. I will teach you the good and right way.
Only fear the Lord and serve him faithfully with all your heart and all your soul, and see what great things he does for you.
But if you continue to do evil, both you and your king will die.
And when [?] one year and two, Saul reigned as king over Israel.

Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand were with his son Jonathan at Ramah in Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people away, each to his own home.
Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Saul sounded the trumpet throughout the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!”
And all Israel [?] that Saul had struck the Philistine garrison and that Israel had overcome the Philistines. The people gathered behind Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel, with three thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore, a very great multitude. They came up and camped at Michmash, east of Bethel.
The men of Israel saw this and were afraid. They hid in caves, hollows, rocky clefts, pits, and cisterns.
The Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people were with him.
He waited seven days, until the time set by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people scattered away from Saul.
Saul said, “Bring me the burnt offering.” And he offered sacrifices of well-being as a burnt offering.
When he finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to meet him and greet him.

Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul answered, “I saw that the people were scattering away from me, that you had not come at the appointed time, and that the Philistines were gathered at Michmash.”
I said, ‘The Philistines may come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the Lord’s favor.’ So I took the liberty of offering the burnt offering.

Samuel said to Saul, “You have acted foolishly by not keeping the command that the LORD your God gave you. For now the LORD your God had established your kingdom over Israel and said that he would establish you forever.”

Now your kingdom will not endure, because the Lord has chosen for himself a man after his own heart. The Lord has appointed him to lead his people, because you have not kept everything that the Lord your God commanded you.
Samuel got up and went from Gilgal to Ramah in Benjamin. Saul counted the people who remained with him, about six hundred men.
Saul and his son Jonathan were staying at Gibeah in Benjamin, while the Philistines were camped at Michmash.
Raiding parties went out from the Philistine camp in three companies. One company went along the road to Ophrah, toward the land of Shual.
Another company went along the road to Beth-horon, and another turned toward the border road overlooking the Valley of Zeboim and the wilderness.
No blacksmith could be found anywhere in the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not make swords or spears.”
All Israel went down to the Philistines, each to sharpen his sickle, plowshare, pickaxe, and goad.
There was a broad file for the sickle, the plowshare, the [?], and the pickaxe, and for straightening the goad.
On the day of battle, no sword or spear was found in the hands of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
The Philistine garrison went out to the pass at Michmash.
One day Jonathan, Saul’s son, said to the young man carrying his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistine garrison on the other side.” But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying on the outskirts of Ramah, under the pomegranate tree in Gibeon. About six hundred men were with him.
Ahijah son of Ahitub, the brother of Ichabod [?], son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the LORD’s priest in Shiloh, was carrying the ephod. The people did not know that Jonathan had gone
to the crossing place and wanted to cross over to the Philistine outpost. There was a rocky crag on one side and another rocky crag on the other. One was named Bozez, and the other was named Seneh.
One crag extended from the north opposite Michmash, and the other from the south opposite Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man carrying his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will help us, for nothing prevents the LORD from saving by many or by few.”
His armor-bearer said to him, “Do whatever is in your heart. Turn and go ahead. Here I am with you; do whatever is in your heart.”
Jonathan said to him, “Look, we will cross over to the men and show ourselves to them.
If they say to us, ‘Stay still until we reach you,’ we will stand where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say to us, ‘Come up to us,’ we will go up, because the LORD our God has handed them over to us. This will be our sign.”
Both of them showed themselves to the Philistine outpost. The Philistines said, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they were hiding!”

The men of the outpost called to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up to us, and we will teach you something!” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, “Come up behind me, because the LORD has handed them over to Israel.”
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. The Philistine outpost fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed behind him, killing them.
In the first attack made by Jonathan and his armor-bearer, about twenty men fell, like [?] and like furrows made by a plow in a field.
Panic spread from the camp in the field and through all the troops stationed there. The raiders also trembled, and the earth shook. Terror from the LORD fell upon them.
Saul’s lookouts in Gibeah of Benjamin saw that the Philistine army was shaking, moving away, and breaking apart.
Saul said to the people with him, “Count and see who has gone from us.” They counted and saw that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God here,” for the ark of the LORD was there that day with the Israelites.
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the force in the Philistine camp kept increasing. Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”
Saul and all the people with him shouted and came to the battle. There, each man’s sword was turned against his companion, and there was tremendous confusion.
The Hebrews and Philistines who, as in previous days, had gone up with them to the camp and were stationed around it also joined the Israelites, Saul, and Jonathan.
All the men of Israel who were hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled before the Israelites. They too armed themselves and followed them into battle.
The LORD saved Israel that day and fought a battle for them at Beth-aven,
for the men of Israel. Saul fought that day and said to the people, “Cursed is anyone who eats food before evening, before I have taken revenge on my enemies.” So none of the people tasted food.
They went throughout the land and entered the forest. There was honey in the forest, on the surface of the ground.
The people entered the forest, where honey was flowing, but no one put his hand to his mouth, because the people feared the oath.
Jonathan had not heard his father put the people under oath. He extended the tip of the staff in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, and brought his hand back to his mouth. His eyes brightened.
A man from the people answered Jonathan, “Your father put the people under a solemn oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’” And the people were exhausted.
Jonathan said, “My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
And because the people have not eaten today from the plunder they found belonging to their enemies, the slaughter among the Philistines has not been great.”
We struck down the Philistines today from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very exhausted.
The people rushed upon the plunder and took sheep, oxen, and calves. They slaughtered them on the ground, and the people ate them with the blood.
They reported to Saul, saying, “Look, the people have sinned against the LORD by eating with the blood.” Saul said, “You have acted faithlessly. Cut me a large stone today.”

Saul said, “Go around among the people and tell them, ‘Each man must bring his ox or his sheep and slaughter it here. Do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.’” So that night all the people brought their oxen, each leading his own, and slaughtered them there.
Saul built an altar to the LORD there, and he began to build an altar to the LORD.
Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines and plunder them until morning light. Let us not leave a single man among them.” They said, “We will do whatever seems good to you.”
Saul said to God, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you deliver them into Israel’s hands?” But the LORD did not answer him that day.
Saul said, “Bring all the tribes of the people here to me. Find out and see how this sin happened today.”
“As surely as the LORD lives, who has saved Israel, even if it is in my son Jonathan, he must certainly die.” But no one among all the people answered him.
He said to all Israel, “You stand on one side, and my son Jonathan and I will stand on the other side.” The people said to Saul, “Do whatever seems good to you.”
Saul said, “LORD, God of Israel, give a true decision.” Saul and Jonathan were selected, and the people were cleared.
Saul said, “Cast lots between me and my son Jonathan.” And Jonathan was selected.
Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” Jonathan told him, “With the tip of the staff in my hand, I tasted a little honey. For that I must die.”
Saul said, “May God do this to me, and more besides, if you do not surely die, Jonathan.”

The people said to Saul, “Must Jonathan die, who brought deliverance to Israel? Never! As the LORD God lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, for he brought deliverance today with God’s help.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.
Saul turned back from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own land.
Saul took control of the kingdom of Israel and fought against all his enemies around him: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kingdom of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he was victorious.
He gathered an army, struck down Amalek, and rescued Israel from the hands of its plunderers.
These were Saul’s sons: Jonathan, Ishvi, Malchishua, and Ishbashul [?]. The names of his two daughters were Nadab, the older, and Michal, the younger.
Saul’s wife was named Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of his army was named Abner son of Ner, Saul’s uncle.
Kish was Saul’s father, and Ner son of Abiel was Abner’s father.
There was fierce warfare with the Philistines throughout Saul’s lifetime. Whenever Saul saw a mighty man or a man of strength, he recruited him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, “The LORD sent me to anoint you to reign over his people Israel. Now listen to the words of the LORD.”
This is what the Lord of hosts says: “I remember what Amalek did to Israel on the road when they were coming up from Egypt.
Now go and destroy the sinful Amalekites. Destroy everything they have, and do not spare them. Kill men and women, young people and infants, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys.”
Saul summoned all the people to battle and counted them at Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand with the men of Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek and camped in the valley.

Saul said to the Kenites, “Turn aside, leave, and come down from among the Amalekites, so that I do not destroy you with them. You showed kindness to the whole house of Israel when they were coming up from Egypt.” So the Kenites withdrew from among the Amalekites.
Saul struck down Amalek from Havilah, at the approach to Shur [?], opposite Egypt.
He captured Agag, king of Amalek, alive, but destroyed all the people with the sword.

Saul and the people spared King Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat animals and the fattened animals, and everything good. They were unwilling to destroy them. But everything they considered worthless and despised, they destroyed.
The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying:
“I regret making Saul king, because he has turned away from following me and has not carried out my words.” Samuel was distressed and prayed before the Lord all night.
Samuel rose early in the morning to meet Saul. Samuel was told, “Saul has come to Carmel, and there he is preparing a place for himself. Then he turned, passed on, and went down to Gilgal.”
Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, “Blessed is the Lord, who has fulfilled his word.”
Samuel said to Saul, “What is this sound of sheep in my ears, and the sound of cattle that I hear?”
Saul said, “They brought them from Amalek, because the people spared the best of the sheep and cattle and brought them to sacrifice to the Lord your God. We destroyed the rest.”
Samuel said to Saul, “Be quiet, and I will tell you what the Lord said to me last night.” Saul said to him, “Speak.”
Samuel said to Saul, “Look, although you are small in your own eyes, you are the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed you to reign over Israel.
The Lord sent you on a journey and said, ‘Go and destroy the sinful Amalekites. Fight against them until you have wiped them out.’
Why did you not obey the Lord’s voice? Instead, you turned to the plunder and did what was evil before the Lord.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I did obey the Lord’s voice and went on the journey on which he sent me. I brought back Agag, king of Amalek, and destroyed the Amalekites.
But the people took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of what was devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the Lord your God at Gilgal.”
Samuel said, “The Lord does not desire burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as obedience to his voice. Look, obedience is better than sacrifices, and listening is better than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is the sin of divination, and stubbornness is wicked divination. Because you have rejected the Lord’s word, he will reject you as king.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, because I disobeyed the word from the Lord’s mouth and your words. I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
Now forgive my sin and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you. Because you have rejected the Lord’s word, the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel.”
Samuel turned to leave, and Saul seized the edge of his robe and tore it.
Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel away from you today and given it to your companion, who is better than you.”
“Moreover, the Triumphant One of Israel does not lie or change his mind, because he is not a human being who changes his mind.”
Saul said, “I have sinned. Now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me so that I may worship the LORD your God.”
Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.
Samuel said, “Bring Agag king of Amalek here to me.” Agag said, “Death is truly bitter.”
Samuel said, “Just as your sword has bereaved women of their children, so your mother will be bereaved among women.” Samuel cut King Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.
Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Ramah of Saul.
Samuel never again saw Saul until the day he died, for Samuel mourned over Saul. And the LORD regretted making Saul king over Israel.

The LORD said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn over Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and come. I will send you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have found a king for myself among his sons.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? Saul will hear about it and kill me.” The LORD said to Samuel, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.’”
“Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what to do. Anoint for me the one I tell you to anoint.”
Samuel did as the Lord commanded him and came to Bethlehem in Judah. The elders of the town came out to meet him.

They said, “Do you come in peace?” He said, “In peace. I have come to sacrifice to the Lord. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” He consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they came, he saw Eliab and said, “The LORD’s anointed is like him.”

The Lord said to Samuel, “Do not look at his appearance or the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For I do not see as a human sees: a human looks with the eyes, but the Lord looks at the heart.”
Jesse called Abinadab and had him pass before Samuel. Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse had Shammah pass before him, and Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse had seven of his sons pass before Samuel. Samuel said to Jesse, “The LORD has not chosen these.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are these all the boys?” He answered him, “The youngest is still left; he is tending the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send for him and bring him, because I will not return until he comes here.”
He sent for him and brought him. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. The LORD said to Samuel, “Get up and anoint him, for this is the one.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him among his brothers. The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon David from that day onward. Samuel rose early and went to his home in Ramah.
The Spirit of God departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD tormented him.
Saul’s servants said to him:
“Here are your servants before you. Let them look for a man who knows how to play the lyre. When the evil spirit comes upon you, he will play with his hands, and you will feel better.”
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a man who plays well and bring him to me.”
One of the young men answered, “I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play. He is a brave and mighty man, a warrior, discerning in speech, and handsome, and the LORD is with him.”
King Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Send me your son David; I need him.”
Jesse took a donkey and loaded it with bread, a wineskin of wine, and a young goat. He sent them to Saul with his son David.
David came to Saul and entered his service. Saul loved him greatly, and David became his armor-bearer.
Saul sent word to Jesse and said to him, “Let David remain in my service, because he has found favor in my eyes.”
Whenever the evil spirit of the Lord came upon Saul, David would take the lyre and play it. Saul would be relieved and feel better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for battle and fought at Suph in Judah. They camped between Suph and Beth-arqa, in Apharsamin.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered and camped in the Valley of Elah, and they drew up their battle line against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on the hill on one side, and Israel stood on the hill on the other side, with the valley between them.
A mighty warrior came out from the Philistine camp, named Goliath, from Gath. He was six cubits and a span tall.
He had a bronze helmet on his head and wore a coat of scale armor. His armor weighed five thousand shekels of bronze.
He had bronze shin guards on his legs and a bronze shield between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and his spearhead weighed six hundred shekels of iron. His shield-bearer walked ahead of him.

He stood and called out to the ranks of Israel, saying to them, “Why have you come out to form a battle line? Look, I am a Philistine, and you are Saul’s servants. Choose a man for yourselves to come out against me.
If he can fight me and kill me, we will be your slaves. But if I defeat him and kill him, you will be our slaves and serve us.”
The Philistine said, “Today I have defied the ranks of Israel. Give me a man so that we can fight each other.”
Saul and all Israel heard the Philistine’s words, and they trembled and were very afraid.
David was the son of an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah, whose name was Jesse. He had eight sons, and in Saul’s days the man was old and advanced in years.
Jesse’s three oldest sons had followed Saul to battle. Their names were Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab his second, and Shammah the third.
David was the youngest.
David had returned from Saul and gone to tend his father’s sheep in Bethlehem.
The Philistine came forward morning and evening and took his stand for forty days.
Jesse said to his son David, “Take a seah of roasted grain and ten loaves of bread to your brothers, and hurry to your brothers in the camp.
Take these ten cheeses made from milk to the commander of the thousand. Check on your brothers’ well-being and bring me news of them.”
Saul and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines.

David got up early in the morning, left the sheep with the keepers, took the provisions, and went as Jesse had instructed him. He came to the camp at the valley as the army was going out to form the battle line, and they raised the battle cry.
Israel and the Philistines drew up their battle lines, one facing the other.
David set down the things he was carrying beside the baggage, ran to the battle line, and asked his brothers how they were.
While he was speaking with them, the mighty warrior came up from the Philistine ranks—the Philistine from Gath named Goliath. He spoke these same words, and David heard him.
When all the men of Israel saw the champion, they were afraid and fled from him.

The men of Israel said, “Have you seen this man? He has come up to insult Israel. The king will give great wealth to the man who kills him, give him his daughter, and make his father’s household free in Israel.”

David said to the men standing beside him, “What will be done for the man who kills this uncircumcised Philistine and removes the disgrace from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he insults the ranks of the living God?”
The people answered him in the same way, saying, “This is what will be done for the man who kills him.”

His oldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men. Eliab became furious with David and said to him, “Why have you come down? With whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your insolence and the wickedness of your heart. You have come down just to watch the battle.”
David said, “What have I done now? It was only a word!”
He turned away from him toward someone else and asked the same question, and the people gave him the same answer as before.
The words David had spoken reached Saul, and he had him brought in.
David said to Saul, “Let no one lose heart because of him. Your servant will go and fight this Philistine.”
Saul said to David, “You cannot go against this Philistine to fight him, because you are a boy, and he has been a warrior since his youth.”
David said to Saul, “Your servant was tending sheep for my father, and a lion and a wolf came and took a lamb from the flock.
I went after it, struck it, and rescued the lamb from its mouth. It turned on me in fury, and I caught it by its beard, struck it, and [?].
Your servant has killed both a lion and a wolf. This uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has insulted the ranks of the living God.”
David said, “The Lord, who rescued me from the power of the lion and the wolf, will rescue me from the hands of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go, and may the Lord be with you.”
Saul dressed David in his own clothing, put a bronze helmet on his head, and clothed him in armor.
David strapped his sword on over his clothing, but he was unwilling to walk because he had not tried them before. So David took them off.
He took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the streambed, and put them in his shepherd’s bag, in his pouch. With his sling in his hand, he approached the Philistine.
The Philistine came forward and approached David, with the man carrying his shield ahead of him.
The Philistine looked closely at David and despised him, because he was a ruddy, handsome boy.
The Philistine said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come against me with a staff?” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, “Come here, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the wild animals.”
David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with a sword, a spear, and a shield, but I come against you in the name of the Lord, the God of hosts, whose ranks of Israel you have insulted.

Today the Lord will hand you over to me. I will kill you and cut off your head. Today I will give the corpses of the Philistine army to the wild animals and the birds of the sky, and the whole earth will know that Israel has a God.
This whole assembly will know that the Lord does not save by sword or spear, for the battle belongs to the Lord, and he will hand you over to us.”
The Philistine came forward and approached to meet David, and David hurried and ran toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.
David reached into his bag, took out a stone, swung his sling, and struck the Philistine between the eyes. The stone sank in between his eyes, and he fell facedown on the ground.
David overpowered the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He struck the Philistine and killed him, though David had no sword in his hand.
David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it from its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

The men of Israel and Judah rose up, took courage, and pursued the Philistines as far as the entrance to the valley and as far as the valley of Ekron. The slain Philistines fell along the road to Shaaraim, as far as Gath and as far as Ekron.
The Israelites returned from pursuing the Philistines and plundered their camps.
David took the Philistine’s head and brought it to Jerusalem, and he put his equipment in his tent.
When Saul saw David going out to meet the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of his army, “Whose son is this young man?” Abner said, “As you live, Your Majesty, I do not know.”
The king said, “Find out whose son this young man is.”
When David returned after killing the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul, with the Philistine’s head in his hand.
Saul said to him, “Whose son are you, young man?” David said to him, “I am the son of your servant Jesse from Bethlehem.”
When David finished speaking to Saul, Jonathan’s soul became bound to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him as himself.
Saul took him into his service that day and did not let him return to his father’s house.
Jonathan and David made a covenant because Jonathan loved David as himself.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with the equipment he wore, including his sword, his bow, and his belt.
David went wherever Saul sent him and was victorious. Saul put him in command of the fighting men, and this pleased the people as well as Saul’s servants.

As they were coming back, when David returned after killing the Philistine, women came out from all the towns of Israel to sing praises with four-stringed instruments and to meet King Saul with tambourines, cymbals, and joy.
The women sang in response to one another, rejoicing and saying, “Saul has killed thousands, and David tens of thousands.”
Saul became very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, “David has been given tens of thousands, while I have been given thousands. Next the kingdom will be his!”
From that day on, Saul began to look at David with suspicion.
Some days later, an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he prophesied inside his house. David was playing music before him, as he did every day, and Saul had a spear in his hand.
Saul threw the spear, saying, “I will strike David and pin him to the wall.” But David dodged away from him twice.
Saul was afraid of David because the Lord was with him but had departed from Saul.
Saul removed him from his presence and made him commander of a thousand men. David went out and came in at the head of the people.
David acted wisely in all his ways, and the Lord was with him.
Saul saw that David was very wise, and he was afraid of him.
All Israel and Judah loved David because he went out and came in at their head.

Saul said to David, “Here is my older daughter Nadab. I will give her to you as your wife. Only be a commander for me and fight the Lord’s battles.” Saul said, “Let my hand not be against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.”
David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what have I done? What is my life, and what is my father’s family in Israel, that I should marry the king’s daughter?”
When the time came to give Saul’s daughter Nadab to David, she was given as a wife to Azriel of Meholah.
Saul’s daughter Michal loved David. They told Saul, and the matter pleased him.

Saul said, “I will give her to him, and she will be a snare for him, so that the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” Saul said to David, “Through both of them you will become my son-in-law today.”
Saul commanded his servants to say to David son of Jesse, “Look, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now become the king’s son-in-law.”
Saul’s servants spoke these words to David. David said, “Do you consider it a small thing for me to become the king’s son-in-law, when I am a poor and insignificant man?”
Saul’s servants reported to him and told him these words that David had spoken.

Saul said, “This is what you must say to David: ‘The king wants no bride-price except two hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on his enemies.’” King Saul was planning to make David fall into the hands of the Philistines.
Saul’s servants told David these words, and David was pleased at the prospect of becoming the king’s son-in-law. Before the allotted days were over,

David set out with his men and killed two hundred Philistine men. David brought their foreskins and presented them to the king so that he could become the king’s son-in-law. Saul gave him his daughter Michal as his wife.
Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with David, and that Saul’s daughter Michal loved David very much.
Saul became still more afraid of David, and Saul was David’s enemy all his days.
The Philistine commanders went out to battle, and whenever they went out, David had greater success than all Saul’s servants. His name became highly honored.
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Saul’s son Jonathan was very fond of David.
Jonathan told David, “My father Saul is seeking to kill you. Be on your guard, stay in a hiding place, and keep yourself hidden.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are. I will speak to my father about you, see what he thinks, and tell you.”
Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul and said to him, “The king must not sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and his deeds have benefited you.

He put his life in your hands and killed the Philistine, and through him the Lord brought about a great deliverance for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why then are you now sinning against innocent blood and killing David [?] without cause?”
Saul listened to his son Jonathan, and Saul swore, “As the Lord lives, he will not be put to death.”
Jonathan called David and told him all these things. He brought him to Saul, and David was with him as he had been before.
War broke out again, and David went out and fought the Philistines. He struck them with a great blow, and they fled before him.
An evil spirit from the Lord came upon Saul as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand, while David played music before him.
Saul tried to drive the spear through David into the wall, but David escaped from Saul, and Saul drove the spear into the wall. David fled and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him and kill him in the morning. David’s wife Michal warned him, saying, “Unless you save your life, you will be dead tomorrow.”
Michal lowered David through the window, and he fled, went away, and escaped.
Michal took an idol and laid it in the bed. She placed a goatskin at its head and covered it with a blanket.
Saul sent messengers to bring David, but she said, “He is sick.”
Saul sent messengers to see David and said, “Bring him up to me in his bed so that I can kill him.”
The messengers came, and there was an idol in the bed, with a goatskin at its head. They reported this to Saul.
Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me like this and sent my enemy away so that he escaped?” Michal said to Saul, “He told me, ‘Let me go, or I will kill you.’”
David fled and escaped. He came to Samuel at Ramah and told him everything Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went and stayed at Naioth in Ramah.
They told Saul, “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul sent messengers to seize David. They saw a group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing over them. The Spirit of God came upon Saul’s messengers, and they too prophesied.
They told Saul, and he sent other messengers again, and they too prophesied. Saul sent messengers yet again, a third group, and they too prophesied.
He himself also went to Ramah and reached the great cistern in Suph. Saul asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” They told him, “They are at Naioth in Ramah.”
He went there, to Naioth in Ramah. The Spirit of God came upon him too, and he went along prophesying until he reached Naioth in Ramah.
He too stripped off his clothes and prophesied before Samuel. He fell down naked and lay there all that day and all that night. That is why people say, “Look, Saul too is among the prophets!”
David fled from Naioth in Ramah. He came and said to Jonathan, “What have I done? What is my guilt, and what offense have I committed against your father, that he seeks my life?”
Jonathan said to him, “Far from it! You will not die. My father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. Why would my father hide this matter from me? It cannot be!”

David swore to him and said, “Your father knows that I have found favor with you, so he has said, ‘Jonathan must not know about this, or he will be distressed.’ But as surely as the Lord lives and as you live, there is only a step between me and death.”
Jonathan said to David, “Whatever you wish, I will do for you.”
David said to Jonathan, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and I am certainly expected to sit down to eat with your father. But let me go and hide in the field until the third evening.
If your father notices my absence, tell him, ‘David earnestly asked my permission to go to Bethlehem, his hometown, because the whole clan has its annual sacrifices there.’
If he says, ‘Very well,’ your servant will be safe. But if he becomes angry, know that he has determined to do harm.
Show this kindness to your servant, because you have brought your servant into a covenant with you before the Lord. If I am guilty, kill me yourself, but do not take me to your father.”
Jonathan said, “Far from it! If I learn that my father has determined to bring harm upon you, I will tell you.”
David said to Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?”
Jonathan said to David, “Come, let us go out into the field.” So they both went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, “May the Lord, the God of Israel, be witness! I will sound out my father tomorrow about this time, at the third hour. If he is well disposed toward you, I will send word and let you know.
May the Lord do this to Jonathan, and more besides, if my father intends harm against you and I do not tell you and send you away to go in peace. May the Lord be with you as he was with my father.
And while I am still alive, please show me the kindness of God before I die.
Never withdraw your kindness from my household, even when the Lord destroys David’s enemies from the face of the earth.
May Jonathan stand with David’s household, and may the Lord call David’s enemies to account.”
Jonathan again made David swear because he loved him, for he loved him as he loved his own life.
Jonathan said to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed because your seat will be empty.
After three hours you will be eagerly sought. Come to the place where you hid on the following day, and sit beside that stone.
“And I will aim three arrows to shoot at a target.”

I will send the boy, saying, ‘Go, gather the arrows.’ If I tell the boy, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you; pick them up and come,’ then know and see that you are safe and there is no danger, as the Lord lives.
But if I tell the boy, ‘Look, the arrow is beyond you,’ then go, for the Lord has sent you away.
As for the matter that you and I have spoken about, the Lord God is between you and me forever.”
David hid in the field. When the new moon came, the king reclined at the meal to eat.
The king reclined in his usual place beside the wall. Jonathan rose and reclined, and Abner was beside Saul, but David’s place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day, for he thought, “Something has happened. Perhaps he is clean, or perhaps he was not clean.”
On the next day of the new moon, David’s place was empty again. Saul said to his son Jonathan, “Why has the son of Jesse not come to the meal, either yesterday or today?”
Jonathan answered his father Saul, “David earnestly asked my permission to go to Bethlehem.

He said, ‘Let me go, because we have a family sacrifice in the town, and my brother has instructed me and spoken to me about it. If I have found favor in your eyes, let me go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.”

Saul’s anger flared against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of an undisciplined woman! Do I not know that you favor the son of Jesse, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be secure. Now send and bring him to me, for he deserves to die.”
Jonathan answered his father Saul, “Why should he die? What has he done?”
Saul raised his spear against him to strike him. Then Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David.
Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate nothing that second day of the new moon, because he was grieved over David, since his father had decreed this against him.
In the morning Jonathan went out to the field to meet David, with a young boy accompanying him.
He said to the boy, “Run and gather the arrows that I shoot.” The boy ran, and Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy reached the place where Jonathan’s arrow had fallen, Jonathan called to the boy and said, “Look, the arrow is beyond you!”
